blocks.prompt: The Bird That Gave Up the Sky
blocks.text: Most birds fly away when they are scared. The emu does not. The emu is far too big to fly. It is the tallest bird in Australia. Its wings are tiny. They are about as small as your hand. But the emu has long, strong legs. It can run as fast as a car in town. An emu has three toes on each foot. It swallows small stones. The stones sit in its belly and help grind up its food. A mother emu can make a deep booming drum sound from a pouch in her throat. You can hear it from far away.

blocks.prompt: The Dad Who Sat Still
blocks.text: An emu is not built for the sky. It is built for the ground. A grown emu stands about six feet tall, taller than most adults, and it can run thirty miles an hour without wearing out. Its wings are only about eight inches long. It holds them out like little sails to help it steer, and lifts them to let heat escape on a hot day. The strangest part of an emu's life is what the father does. The mother lays her big dark green eggs in a nest on the ground. Then she walks away. The father sits down on the eggs and stays there for about eight weeks. He barely eats. He barely drinks. He turns the eggs with his beak and waits. By the time the striped chicks hatch, he has lost about a third of his weight. Then he raises them by himself, sometimes for more than a year, chasing off anything that comes too close.

blocks.prompt: The War Australia Lost to a Bird
blocks.text: In 1932, the Australian army went to war with emus and lost. To understand how, you first need to understand the bird. Emus are nomads. They do not guard a patch of land the way most birds do. Instead they walk, sometimes hundreds of miles, following rain clouds toward whatever grass and seed has just come up. A flock of emus is not a neighborhood. It is a moving crowd that arrives, eats, and leaves. That habit ran straight into wheat. Farmers in Western Australia had planted grain across country the emus had been crossing for thousands of years. When drought pushed the birds inland toward the new fields, tens of thousands of them walked through the fences and into the crop. The farmers asked for soldiers. The government sent Major Meredith and two machine guns. It should have been simple. It was not. The emus scattered the moment the guns opened up, splitting into small groups that ran in different directions at thirty miles an hour. One gun was mounted on a truck, and the ground was so rough that the shooting shook wildly and hit almost nothing. After several weeks and thousands of rounds, the soldiers had far less to show for it than anyone had promised, and the operation was called off. Newspapers named it the Emu War, and they agreed on the winner. The joke works because everyone expected a slow, silly bird. What the guns actually met was a fast, nomadic survivor that had been walking that ground long before the fences arrived.

blocks.prompt: Built for the Ground
blocks.text: Look at an emu's wing and you are looking at an argument that ended a long time ago. It is about eight inches of feathers on a bird that stands six feet tall, and it will never lift anything. Flight is expensive. It demands a deep keel on the breastbone, enormous flight muscles, bones hollowed out for lightness, and a body kept small enough to leave the ground. An animal that gives all of that up gets the savings back somewhere else. The emu spent its savings on legs. Those legs carry a bird that can hold thirty miles an hour and keep holding it. Each foot has three toes, and the thick pads underneath work like running shoes on baked ground. The wings did not vanish completely. An emu holds them out from its body while sprinting, which helps it turn, and lifts them to let heat escape when the day is brutal. The feathers are unusual too. Each quill splits into two shafts of almost equal length, so the coat hangs loose and shaggy and lets air move through it instead of trapping heat against the skin. Then there is the nesting, which turns the usual bird story inside out. The female emu is the larger bird, and she does the courting. She booms, a low drum from an inflatable pouch in her throat that carries for more than a mile. Once she has laid her clutch of heavy dark green eggs, she may walk off to find another male and lay again. The father stays. For about eight weeks he sits on the nest, turning the eggs, drinking almost nothing, eating almost nothing, living off his own body until he has lost roughly a third of his weight. When the striped chicks hatch, he raises them alone. Emus are also gardeners, though nobody hired them. They swallow fruit whole and walk for days before the seeds pass through, still alive and ready to grow. Some Australian plants are spread across the country almost entirely on emu time. A bird that cannot fly moves the forest around anyway.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Dromaius novaehollandiae
Ratite: no keel on the breastbone
DNA places the flying tinamou inside the ratite tree
Flightlessness evolved several times, independently
Female booms and courts; male incubates for eight weeks
The Emu War of 1932 was called off as a failure

blocks.prompt: The Emu's Long Argument With the Sky
blocks.text: The emu is a bird that lost an argument with the sky, and it is worth asking whether it lost or simply walked away. Emus belong to a group called the ratites: ostriches, rheas, cassowaries, kiwis, and the extinct moa and elephant birds. For most of the last century the tidy explanation was that these birds shared one flightless ancestor stranded when the southern supercontinent broke apart, each population drifting away on its own landmass to become its own giant. It is a beautiful story. The DNA does not support it. When biologists sequenced the ratites, they found the tinamou, a small partridge-like South American bird that flies perfectly well, sitting deep inside the ratite family tree. A flying bird cannot be nested among flightless relatives unless flight was lost more than once. The best reading of the evidence now is that flightlessness evolved independently, several separate times, in birds that had already spread by air and then discovered they no longer needed it. That reframes the emu. It is not a failure of flight. It is a bird whose ancestors did the math and stopped paying. Flight is the most expensive thing a vertebrate can do. It requires a deep keel on the breastbone to anchor flight muscles that can account for a fifth of body weight, bones hollowed out for lightness, and a strict ceiling on how large the animal is allowed to get. Give all of that up on a continent with few large ground predators and the budget frees up at once. The emu spent it on legs. A modern emu stands close to six feet tall, weighs up to about a hundred pounds, and cruises at thirty miles an hour on three-toed feet. Its wing has shrunk to roughly eight inches, but it was not thrown away. The bird holds it out as a rudder when it turns at speed and raises it to dump heat on a bad day. Even the feathers are rebuilt for ground life: each quill carries two shafts of nearly equal length, so the plumage hangs loose and shaggy and lets air pass through rather than sealing it in. The breeding is stranger than the running. The female is the bigger bird and does the pursuing, booming a low drum through an inflatable pouch in her throat that carries more than a mile. She lays a clutch of dark green eggs the size of a fist, and then, often, she leaves to find another male and lay again. The father takes the nest and does not get up. For roughly eight weeks he sits, turning the eggs, barely eating, barely drinking, burning his own body for fuel until he has lost about a third of his weight. Then he raises the striped chicks alone, sometimes for more than a year. All of that ground-level living has a consequence people rarely credit. Emus are nomads. They follow rain across hundreds of miles, swallowing fruit whole, and the seeds pass through them intact days later and far away. Several Australian plants depend on emus to move their seeds at all. The bird that gave up the sky spends its life quietly rearranging the ground. Which makes the events of 1932 look less like comedy and more like a misunderstanding. When drought drove tens of thousands of emus into the new wheat farms of Western Australia, the government sent soldiers with machine guns to settle it. The emus scattered, split, and ran, and after weeks of shooting the operation was quietly abandoned. Newspapers named it the Emu War and gave the win to the birds. The joke lands because we expected a slow, stupid animal. What actually met the guns was a fast, nomadic, drought-tracking survivor that had been crossing that ground since long before the fences.
